claims.claim: Display term: Specific phobia. Plain-English subtitle: Intense, disproportionate fear of mice and rats. This uses the clinical category of specific phobia for an animal-related fear, not a separate invented diagnosis.

Encountering the feared animal or anticipating an encounter may provoke intense fear, anxiety and active avoidance; the shed encounter is an illustrative fictional example, not a clinical case or universal trigger.
Anticipatory anxiety means worry before an encounter; even thinking about feared situations can cause anxiety and avoidance.
Autonomic arousal is the body alarm associated with fear; noticeable heartbeat and trembling can occur, but symptoms vary.

Negative reinforcement can maintain avoidance: short-term relief after avoiding a feared situation can make avoidance more likely again; this is a possible learning mechanism, not an explanation of every case.
Specific phobia involves fear out of proportion to actual danger; ordinary caution around animals is distinct from disabling phobic fear.

Mice and rats can carry germs and small mammals can bite. Be cautious with unfamiliar animals; wash hands after handling small mammals or their supplies. Therapy does not mean ignoring genuine animal-related hazards.

CBT is evidence-based treatment; exposure therapy is a particularly effective CBT method for phobias, with a clinician and patient able to plan work on avoided situations. Seek professional help when fear affects daily life.
Illustrated help is a collaborative conversation about an animal photograph, not instructions to approach or handle wild rodents; treatment can help and is individualized.

CBT is a treatment for phobias; gradual exposure is used for simple phobias, with a plan adapted to the person and specialist help available.

claims.claim: Cats take in water both by drinking and through moisture in their food.
Wet food can contain up to 80% water; cats eating wet food may drink less, while dry-fed cats generally obtain more water by drinking.
Dry cat food contains 6–10% water; canned food contains at least 75% water. These are typical food-format values, not feeding ratios.
Cats should always have access to clean fresh water, even when eating wet food.
Wet food can help increase water intake; a diet should still be complete and balanced.
The bowl alone does not measure total water intake because food contributes water.
If dehydration is suspected, contact a veterinarian promptly; this is general education rather than an individualized intake prescription.

claims.claim: The cornea admits light, the iris regulates entry through the pupil, and the lens focuses incoming light onto the retina; the optic nerve carries visual information toward the brain.
The tapetum lucidum lies behind the retina and reflects light that was not absorbed on its first passage, providing a second opportunity for retinal absorption and improving sensitivity in dim light.
The tapetum is a reflector of incoming light, not a light-producing organ; diagram arrows represent incident and reflected light rather than generated light.

Cat tapetal cells contain ordered groups of slender rodlets; multilayer reflecting domains account for reflection, with reflected wavelength depending on domain layer spacing. Schematic microscopic studies are not to scale.
A tapetal layer is part of the choroidal tissues behind the retina; schematic layers may be simplified and exaggerated for explanation, not represented as a full clinical histology section.

claims.claim: True lilies (Lilium species) and daylilies (Hemerocallis species) can cause potentially fatal kidney failure in cats.
All parts of these plants are hazardous, including stems, leaves, flowers and pollen; vase water is also hazardous.
Cats can be poisoned by chewing plant material, licking pollen from fur while grooming, or drinking lily vase water; small exposures can cause severe harm.
The specific kidney-toxic substance has not been identified; do not depict a known molecule or a specific molecular mechanism.
Early signs may include vomiting, drooling, loss of appetite and reduced activity; do not wait for signs before seeking help.
Suspected ingestion of lily material, pollen or vase water warrants immediate veterinary or pet poison control contact; early veterinary treatment improves prognosis.
Keep these lilies out of cat households; bring a plant photograph or sample to help identification when seeking veterinary care.
Do not induce vomiting unless specifically directed by a veterinarian or poison control professional.
An Easter lily (Lilium longiflorum) is a dangerous true lily; daylilies belong to Hemerocallis, a distinct genus.
Not every plant called lily has the same toxin or risk: peace lilies and calla lilies cause calcium-oxalate irritation rather than this true-lily kidney toxicity; they are not safe to chew.

claims.claim: Bunting is a cat approaching and rubbing its head on a person; cats can also bunt one another.
Cats have scent glands around their cheeks, lips and forehead; facial rubbing deposits chemical signals.
Pheromones are chemical signals used in communication between members of the same species.
Cats rub their faces on familiar objects including doorways; facial scent marking occurs in places where cats are comfortable.

claims.claim: Licking is a normal feline grooming behavior; show a healthy domestic cat grooming its foreleg.
The feline tongue bears backward-facing keratin spines called filiform papillae; depict them pointing toward the throat, not toward the tongue tip.
The large grooming papillae have a scoop-shaped, U-shaped cavity at the tip which wicks saliva by surface tension; this is not a hollow syringe connected to a salivary duct.
During tongue expansion the grooming papillae rotate to stand more erect and increase contact with fur.
The tongue presses and compresses fur during the grooming stroke; papillae deliver saliva deeper into the coat than the tongue surface alone.
Saliva wicked into papilla cavities is released onto hairs by contact during grooming.

claims.claim: Ear position is interpreted together with eyes, whiskers, posture, tail and context; these are contextual cues, not a guaranteed emotion or diagnosis.
Upright ears with half-closed eyes can accompany a relaxed expression.
Forward ears and open eyes can indicate attention or anxiety, rather than reliably meaning happiness.
Flattened ears with whiskers drawn against the face can accompany fear; fear can also involve a low crouch and a tucked or closely wrapped tail.
Ears back and flat with whiskers directed forward can accompany defensive or aggressive communication; ears moving backward with tail lashing can precede petting-induced aggression.
When ears move back and the tail lashes during petting, stop petting and allow a cooling-down period without physical contact. Avoid punishment, restraint or uninvited handling.

claims.claim: Osteoporosis reduces bone mass and structural strength, increasing the risk of broken bones.
With aging, the cortical outer shell thins and the inner trabecular architecture becomes thinner and less connected; comparative cutaways are illustrative schematics, not diagnostic scans.
Bone remodeling removes old bone and forms new bone; bone loss occurs when removal outpaces replacement.
Osteoporosis is often silent until a fracture; hip, spine and wrist are common fracture sites, sometimes after minor trauma.
Vertebral compression fractures may shorten the front of a vertebral body, causing back pain, height loss and a stooped posture; not every spinal fracture is due to osteoporosis.
New severe back pain or pain after a minor fall warrants prompt clinical assessment for a possible fracture rather than self-diagnosis.
Risk factors include older age, estrogen decline after menopause, family history and long-term glucocorticoid use; men can also develop osteoporosis.
Evaluation combines fracture and medical history with bone-density testing; DXA measures bone mineral density, commonly at the hip and spine, and helps assess fracture risk.

Care may include adequate calcium, vitamin D and protein, individually appropriate weight-bearing and resistance exercise, balance work and home fall prevention. Exercise should be tailored to fracture risk.
Clinician-selected medicines can slow bone loss or build bone and reduce fracture risk; treatment is individualized, and nutrition alone is not a substitute for indicated medication.

claims.claim: Hypothyroidism means the thyroid does not make enough thyroid hormones to meet body needs.
The thyroid is a butterfly-shaped gland in the lower front of the neck; it releases thyroid hormones into the blood to reach body tissues.
Thyroid hormones help regulate energy use and warmth and support the brain, heart, muscles and other organs; low levels slow many body functions.
The pituitary releases TSH, which signals the thyroid to work. In primary thyroid failure TSH usually rises as hormone output falls; pituitary disease is an exception.
Hashimoto autoimmune disease attacks the thyroid and is the most common cause of hypothyroidism; thyroid surgery, radiation and some medicines are other causes.
Possible symptoms include fatigue, feeling cold, dry skin, constipation and slowed heart rate; symptoms vary and are not diagnostic alone.
TSH and free T4 blood tests help diagnose hypothyroidism; history and examination help find the cause.
Levothyroxine replaces missing thyroid hormone, with clinician-guided dosing and follow-up blood tests, commonly 6 to 8 weeks after starting or changing a dose.
Do not stop thyroid medicine or change its dose without consulting the clinician.
Excess iodine, including kelp or iodine supplements, can worsen autoimmune thyroid disease; supplements are not a universal fix.
Contact the clinician promptly if pregnant because thyroid hormone needs may change and untreated hypothyroidism can harm mother and baby.
Rare severe untreated hypothyroidism can progress to life-threatening myxedema coma, requiring immediate medical treatment.

claims.claim: Celiac disease is an autoimmune condition: eating gluten triggers an abnormal immune reaction that damages the small intestine.
Gluten occurs in wheat, barley and rye.

Symptoms may include bloating, abdominal pain, diarrhea and fatigue; some people have no symptoms.
Nutrient malabsorption can lead to iron-deficiency anemia and weakening of bones.
Celiac disease has genetic susceptibility and increased risk in close relatives; eating gluten alone does not mean someone will develop it.

Evaluation commonly uses antibody blood tests and small-intestinal biopsy; symptoms alone do not diagnose it. Do not start a gluten-free diet before diagnostic testing without medical advice because this can affect results.
Treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet with dietitian support; for most people it improves symptoms and allows intestinal healing, but is not a cure.
Read food labels, avoid hidden gluten, and follow up with a clinician to assess symptoms and nutritional deficiencies and supplement only if needed.
Persistent symptoms despite a gluten-free diet warrant clinical reassessment.

With diarrhea or vomiting, inability to keep fluids down or bloody diarrhea requires urgent advice; sudden severe abdominal pain requires emergency care. These are general warning signs, not diagnostic signs of celiac disease.
Celiac disease differs from wheat allergy and non-celiac gluten sensitivity.

Atrial Fibrillation — Causes and Risk Factors

claims.claim: Atrial fibrillation (AFib) is an irregular heart rhythm; the two upper chambers are the atria, and the two lower chambers are the ventricles.
In AFib atrial beating is irregular and atria and ventricles do not work together as they should, reducing efficient blood flow from atria to ventricles.
Blood may pool and form clots in the heart; a clot can travel to and block an artery supplying the brain, causing ischemic stroke. This is a possible complication, not inevitable.
The left atrial appendage is a small sac in the wall of the left atrium where clots can form.
AFib may cause fluttering or pounding palpitations, fatigue, shortness of breath, and lightheadedness, or no symptoms.
Risk increases with age; high blood pressure, sleep apnea and excess alcohol are among risk factors, not a single universal cause.
Clinician assessment and an electrocardiogram (ECG/EKG) diagnose AFib; longer monitoring may detect intermittent episodes.

Management can include heart-rate control, rhythm control with medicines, electrical cardioversion or catheter ablation in selected people, and management of underlying risk factors. Treatment is individualized.
Anticoagulants may lower stroke risk when indicated after clinical assessment, but carry bleeding risk; rhythm treatment does not mean stroke-risk assessment can be ignored.
Treating high blood pressure and sleep apnea and discussing alcohol use with a clinician are relevant elements of AFib care.
Call 911 immediately for sudden weakness or trouble speaking, or chest pressure lasting minutes or returning, which can indicate stroke or heart attack. Do not dismiss these as routine AFib symptoms.

claims.claim: The meadow spittlebug, Philaenus spumarius, is a hemipteran; its adult is also called a froghopper.
Meadow spittlebug nymphs are pale green or yellow; lime-green nymphs can have red eyes. Adults are generally tan to brown or gray.
The meadow spittlebug occurs in the North American Midwest and feeds on many herbaceous plants including clover and strawberries.
Both adults and nymphs feed on water-carrying xylem sap; its low nutrient concentration requires processing large quantities.
Hemipteran piercing-sucking mouthparts extend below the head; hoppers have a down-and-back-pointing proboscis. A simplified feeding study can show mouthparts reaching plant sap tissues.
Nymphs feed head downward and excrete excess sap through the anus, not the mouth.
Epidermal gland secretions stabilize foam; air is mixed with excreted fluid as abdominal movements form bubbles.
Nymphs use their legs to pull forming bubbles forward over the body.
The foam conceals nymphs from predators, buffers temperature extremes and helps prevent drying. It is protective, not an invulnerable shield.

In the described temperate life cycle eggs overwinter in plant stems, nymphs hatch in spring, molt as they grow, and become winged adults; females lay eggs in late summer to fall. There is no pupal stage in hemipteran incomplete metamorphosis.
Adult spittlebugs are tiny, under a quarter inch long, and hop between plants; adult wings must not appear on the young nymph.

General insect digestive anatomy has a tube-like alimentary canal running mouth to anus with foregut, midgut and hindgut; midgut nutrient absorption is a generalized function, not a species-specific measured dissection.
The insect body plan has six legs and distinct head, thorax and abdomen; small wingless hemipteran nymphs differ from winged adults.

claims.claim: Social anxiety disorder, also called social phobia, is persistent overwhelming fear of social situations involving possible scrutiny, negative judgment, humiliation or rejection; it is more than ordinary shyness and can impair daily life.

Anticipatory worry before social events and self-critical review afterward can occur.
Symptoms may include blushing, sweating, trembling, rapid heartbeat, nausea and the mind going blank; responses differ among people.
Fearful predictions about others judging or rejecting a person may be distorted or untrue; anxiety is not proof that rejection is occurring.
Avoiding feared social situations can feel helpful briefly, but anxiety is likely to remain without treatment.
CBT with a therapist is a well-supported treatment, addressing patterns of thinking and behavior; graduated exposure is a CBT method that progressively approaches feared activities.
Treatment is tailored with a clinician; medication such as an SSRI may also help some people.

claims.claim: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease: immune activity destroys insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas, causing little or no insulin.
Insulin helps glucose enter body cells for energy; insufficient insulin causes blood glucose to rise. The tissue and glucose symbols are schematic and not to scale.
Type 1 diabetes can develop at any age; family history raises risk.
Common symptoms include frequent urination, thirst, fatigue, unexplained weight loss and blurred vision.
Suspected type 1 diabetes needs urgent medical assessment; diagnosis uses blood glucose tests, with autoantibody tests helping establish the type.

Insulin treatment is essential; insulin pens or pumps and regular glucose monitoring support individualized care with a diabetes team. Healthy eating and activity support management but do not replace insulin.
Too much insulin can cause low blood glucose, so treatment and monitoring require an individualized care plan.
Without enough insulin, fat breakdown produces ketones that can accumulate and cause diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a medical emergency.
Vomiting or abdominal pain, fast deep breathing, fruity breath, sleepiness or confusion may signal DKA; seek emergency care immediately, especially with thirst and frequent urination.

claims.claim: Pneumonia is an infection of one or both lungs; alveoli are air sacs that can fill with fluid or pus.
Bacteria and viruses commonly cause pneumonia; fungi can also cause it.
Symptoms may include cough, fever, chills, shortness of breath, chest pain and tiredness; symptoms vary.
Clinical assessment may include a chest examination, chest X-ray and blood tests; symptoms alone do not establish the diagnosis.
Bacterial pneumonia is usually treated with antibiotics; treatment depends on cause and severity, so antibiotics are not a universal treatment.
Rest and fluids support recovery; severe illness may require hospital care and oxygen.
Severe trouble breathing, blue or pale lips or skin, sudden confusion, or coughing blood require emergency care.
Worsening symptoms need prompt medical assessment.
Recommended vaccines can prevent some infections that cause pneumonia; handwashing and not smoking help reduce risk.
Young children, older adults and people with weakened immunity or chronic lung disease have higher risk.

claims.claim: A peptic ulcer is a sore in the lining of the stomach or duodenum; the two locations are alternatives, not necessarily simultaneous.
Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAID medicines are the most common causes of peptic ulcers.
NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can make the stomach lining more prone to damage and ulcers; this is a risk, not a universal outcome.
Symptoms can include upper abdominal burning or discomfort, feeling full early, nausea and bloating; some people have no symptoms.
Food can relieve pain briefly in some people and worsen it in others; meal timing cannot diagnose an ulcer.
Evaluation may use H. pylori breath or stool tests and sometimes upper gastrointestinal endoscopy.
Treatment targets the cause, including antibiotics for H. pylori infection and acid-reducing medicines such as proton pump inhibitors.
A clinician may review or change NSAID medicines; an infographic should not direct independent changes to prescribed medicines.
Follow-up tests may be needed to confirm treatment has worked.
Ulcers may cause bleeding or perforation; these are possible complications, not present in every ulcer.
Vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, black tarry stool, sudden severe persistent abdominal pain or fainting needs urgent or emergency assessment.
Diet is not considered an important primary cause or treatment for peptic ulcers; foods may worsen symptoms for some people and do not replace treating H. pylori or medication causes.
This infographic provides general education, not a diagnosis or an individualized treatment plan.

claims.claim: Gout is inflammatory arthritis; urate can accumulate and form needle-shaped crystals in joints, triggering painful inflammation.
Urate comes from purine breakdown in body tissues and foods; it normally leaves in urine. Too much production or too little removal can raise blood urate. Not everyone with high urate develops gout.
Gout commonly affects the big toe joint but can affect other joints; a flare causes sudden severe pain, warmth and swelling, sometimes redness that may be harder to see on darker skin.
Genes, kidney disease, alcohol and some medicines can increase gout risk; gout is not simply a consequence of food choices.
First-time symptoms need medical evaluation. Blood urate testing and sometimes joint-fluid crystal testing help evaluate gout.
Clinicians treat flares with anti-inflammatory medicines such as NSAIDs or steroids, selected for individual safety; rest, elevation and a wrapped cold pack can help.
Urate-lowering medicine may be needed for recurrent attacks or high uric acid; take it regularly even when symptom-free. Healthy habits support prevention but do not replace needed medicines.
A suddenly painful swollen joint with worsening pain, fever or chills, or feeling sick needs urgent assessment because joint infection is possible.

claims.claim: Diverticula are pouches that push outward through weak spots in the colon wall, most often in the sigmoid colon.
Diverticulosis means pouches are present; most people with diverticula do not develop symptoms or problems.
Diverticulitis means diverticula become inflamed; this is not an inevitable progression of diverticulosis.
Symptoms can include severe constant abdominal pain, often in the lower left abdomen, and fever; the location is not universal.
Assessment may include blood tests and CT imaging to clarify the diagnosis and distinguish other causes of symptoms.
Uncomplicated diverticulitis may be managed at home under clinician guidance; treatment depends on severity and patient factors.
Treatment may include clinician-selected pain relief and temporary dietary changes; antibiotics are not needed for every person.
Severe disease or complications may need hospital treatment; abscess drainage or surgery can be necessary in selected cases.
A colon-wall perforation or abscess is a possible complication, not the normal appearance of every case.
Worsening persistent pain, fever or vomiting that prevents keeping fluids down warrants prompt medical assessment.
Severe abdominal pain with vomiting, a swollen abdomen or inability to pass stool or gas warrants emergency care.
After the acute episode, clinician-advised fiber intake, physical activity and not smoking may lower future risk; no guaranteed prevention is claimed.
This infographic provides general education, not a diagnosis or an individualized treatment plan.

claims.claim: Retinal rod photoreceptors and the reflective tapetum contribute to vision in dim light; this does not mean vision in total darkness.
The cornea and lens direct incoming light to the retina; the optic nerve carries visual information.
The pupil changes size in response to light.
Mobile pinnae help collect and locate sound; the ear canal, eardrum and cochlea have distinct roles in hearing.
Cats hear higher sound frequencies than humans.
Smell provides information about food, places and other animals.
Mechanical displacement of a whisker stimulates sensory receptors associated with the follicle, not nerves inside the hair shaft.
The semicircular canals are inner-ear balance structures, separate from the cochlea used in hearing.
Backward-facing keratin papillae on the tongue contribute to grooming; these visible spines are not taste buds.

Create ONE elaborate, beautifully artistic, richly detailed feline communication infographic titled "THE QUIET LANGUAGE OF CATS", subtitle "Read the whole cat, not one signal". This is the Body Language plate of an illustrated cat atlas. Render the finished portrait composition itself, directly edge to edge, not a photograph of a poster, book on a table, framed print, room, screen or physical display. Use exquisite observational watercolor and gouache with fine ink, accurate soft fur, subtle expressive anatomy, muted sage, warm ochre, dusty rose and ivory. Every cat must look like a real domestic cat, never anthropomorphic, grinning, dressed up or cartoonish.

Make a large, graceful relaxed domestic shorthair walking toward the viewer with upright tail and a gently curved tip the visual anchor. Let the tail's arc lead naturally into smaller studies arranged as a flowing asymmetrical composition. Build a thoughtful visual narrative through varied scales, open annotations and beautifully integrated close-ups. No rigid rows of identical cards, grids or charts of disembodied emoji faces. Each full-body study must have correct limbs, a single tail, believable posture and naturally coordinated ears, eyes and whiskers. Use a few different natural coat colors to distinguish study subjects without describing breeds.

Core message, elegantly typeset under the title: "Ears + eyes + whiskers + posture + tail + context". A readable small explanatory line: "These are clues, not a fixed emotional code."

Include these meaningful, carefully coordinated visual studies:
- "A FRIENDLY APPROACH": upright tail with soft curved tip, loose posture, ears relaxed. Text: "Often a greeting when the rest of the body is relaxed." Fine leader lines identify the tail curve and soft body posture.
- "RELAXED & COMFORTABLE": a cat resting loosely with neutral ears, relaxed whiskers and softly narrowed eyes. A small eye sequence shows an ordinary slow blink. Text: "Soft eyes and a slow blink can signal comfort." Do not turn this into human smiling.
- "FOCUSED & CURIOUS": a cat leaning gently toward a quiet point of interest, ears aimed forward and whiskers oriented toward it. Text: "Attention follows a sound, scent or movement." Do not equate alertness automatically with happiness.
- "UNEASY — GIVE SPACE": a crouched cat with tense body, ears turned sideways or back and a low tail held close. Text: "Look for a cluster of tension signals." Show concern rather than a monster; no injury, exposed teeth or attack scene is necessary.
- "TOO MUCH CONTACT": a standing or seated cat turning away, body tensing, ears rotating back and tail sweeping firmly. Use two light motion strokes around the tail without duplicating the tail anatomically. Text: "Tail swishing plus tension is a cue to pause." Do not claim every tail movement means anger.
- "BELLY EXPOSED": a loose relaxed cat lying on its back, paws naturally curled. Text: "A sign of comfort can be a greeting—not an invitation to rub the belly." No human hands touching the belly.
- An integrated paired pupil close-up with a small light-and-shadow motif: "PUPILS NEED CONTEXT". Text: "Light changes pupil size; excitement and fear can too." Never label one pupil size as a reliable diagnosis or a single fixed emotion.

Finish with a small graceful takeaway: "Notice patterns. Respect distance. Let the cat choose contact." This is interpretation of body language, not a general care guide, medical diagnosis, disease chart, breed catalog or behavior-training manual. Avoid absolute emotion claims, invented facts, aggressive handling and fear-provoking situations. Keep all main text crisp and naturally phrased, with substantial fine illustrative detail and breathing room. If necessary, omit one secondary study to preserve artistic flow, but keep the whole-body/context principle, the pupil caveat and the belly distinction. Beautiful natural poses and truthful communication matter more than decorative filler.

claims.claim: Cat body signals should be interpreted together and in context, not as a fixed one-signal emotional code.
An upright tail with a softly curved tip and relaxed body often accompanies a friendly greeting.
Soft narrowed eyes and slow blinking can accompany comfort; experiments link slow-blink interactions with positive cat–human communication.
Ears directed forward and whiskers oriented toward an object can accompany interest or attention, not necessarily happiness.
A crouched tense body, ears sideways or back and a closely held tail can form a cluster of unease signals.
During contact, body tension, ears turning back and tail lashing can indicate that interaction should pause.
A relaxed exposed belly is not automatically an invitation to rub it.
Pupil size changes with lighting and can also change with arousal; one pupil size does not identify one emotion.

claims.claim: The appendix is a small pouch attached to the bowel in the lower right abdomen; appendicitis means an infected, swollen appendix.
Blockage by hardened stool or enlarged tissue in the appendix wall are possible causes; in many cases the cause is unclear.
Abdominal pain may start around the belly button, move to the lower right, worsen over hours and worsen with movement or coughing.
Loss of appetite, nausea or vomiting and fever may occur; not everyone has typical symptoms or pain location.
Untreated appendicitis can lead to a burst appendix, peritonitis, abscess or sepsis; these are possible complications, not inevitable outcomes.
Suspected appendicitis requires immediate medical assessment; severe abdominal pain, confusion or difficulty breathing require emergency care.
Diagnosis uses clinical assessment and may include blood and urine tests, ultrasound or CT; no single test always identifies appendicitis and other conditions can cause similar pain.

Usual treatment is surgical removal of the appendix (appendectomy), with antibiotics; selected mild cases may be treated with antibiotics alone under medical supervision, but surgery remains standard care.

claims.claim: Shingles (herpes zoster) is caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus, the same virus that causes chickenpox.
After recovery from chickenpox, virus remains inactive in some nerve cells and may reactivate later; why reactivation occurs in some people is not fully understood.
Reactivated virus travels in a specific nerve, commonly producing a band of rash on one side of the trunk; the face can also be affected.
Risk increases with older age and weakened immunity, including certain diseases and immune-suppressing medicines.
Burning or tingling pain, itching or numbness may precede a red rash; fluid-filled blisters then dry and crust, followed by clearing scabs. Timing varies.
Shingles may be painful or itchy; light touch can provoke intense pain in some people.
Postherpetic neuralgia is pain that persists in the affected area after the rash has gone; older people have a greater chance of developing it.
Blisters on the face require prompt medical attention; blisters near or in the eye can cause lasting eye damage and blindness.
If shingles is suspected, contact a clinician as soon as possible. Early antiviral treatment can shorten illness and reduce severity; pain relief may help.
Cool washcloths, loose clothing, keeping the area clean and avoiding scratching can help with comfort and skin care.
A person cannot catch shingles from another person with shingles. VZV can spread from shingles blisters to susceptible people and cause chickenpox.
VZV spread can occur by direct contact with blister fluid or breathing virus particles from blisters. Virus is not spread before blisters appear or after the rash scabs over.

Cover the rash, avoid touching or scratching it, and wash hands. Avoid contact with susceptible pregnant people, premature or low-birth-weight infants and immunocompromised people until the rash scabs over.

CDC recommends two doses of recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) for adults age 50 and older and adults age 19 and older with weakened immune systems due to disease or therapy, to prevent shingles and related complications.

claims.claim: The retina is light-sensitive tissue lining the back of the eye; it converts entering light into electrical signals sent to the brain through the optic nerve.
Retinal detachment separates the retina from its normal position at the back wall and underlying blood supply, impairing function and risking permanent vision loss.
In the most common, tear-related (rhegmatogenous) type, fluid passes through a retinal hole or tear and collects beneath the retina, lifting it away.
Aging-related separation of vitreous gel from the retina can cause a retinal tear; thinning peripheral retina and trauma can also lead to tears.
Tractional detachment occurs when scar tissue pulls the retina away; diabetes or other conditions can cause it.
Exudative detachment occurs when leaking vessels allow fluid to accumulate beneath the retina; inflammation or abnormal vessels can be involved.
Warning signs include a sudden increase in floaters, flashes of light, and a dark curtain or shadow in the field of vision; some small detachments cause no symptoms.
Retinal detachment is a medical emergency; symptoms require an eye doctor or emergency room right away, and prompt treatment can help protect vision.
Risk factors include extreme nearsightedness, advancing age, previous eye surgery, serious eye injury, previous detachment, and family history; risk factors do not mean detachment is inevitable.
Diagnosis uses a dilated eye exam to inspect the retina, including its periphery; OCT or ultrasound may help when more information is needed.
Laser or freezing treatment can seal retinal tears; a larger detachment may require surgery to put the retina back into place.
A scleral buckle is a silicone band outside the eye wall that pushes it closer to a retinal tear; freezing treatment seals the tear.
Vitrectomy removes vitreous gel and drains fluid from beneath the retina; laser or freezing seals tears and a gas bubble can hold the retina while it heals.
Pneumatic retinopexy uses a gas bubble and specific head posture to position the bubble over a tear, with laser or freezing to seal it.
A retina specialist selects treatment based on the detachment; more than one procedure may be needed and reattachment does not guarantee complete visual recovery.
The macula is the center of the retina; involvement of this central area affects visual prognosis.
Many aging-related detachments cannot be prevented; protective eyewear during risky activities reduces injury risk and regular dilated eye exams can find small tears or detachments early.

claims.claim: Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve at the back of the eye; lost vision cannot be restored by glaucoma treatment.
The optic nerve contains many nerve fibers; loss of these fibers causes blind spots.
Aqueous fluid in the front of the eye normally leaves through the drainage angle; impaired drainage can increase eye pressure.
Open-angle glaucoma develops gradually when the eye does not drain fluid well despite an open angle; it is painless and often has no obvious early symptoms.
High eye pressure increases risk, but some people with high pressure do not develop glaucoma and some have glaucoma at normal pressure.
In angle-closure glaucoma, the iris can block the drainage angle; sudden complete blockage can rapidly raise eye pressure and is an emergency.
Later glaucoma can cause peripheral vision loss and blind spots; illustrative field loss is variable, not a diagnostic simulation.
Older age, a family history of glaucoma and high eye pressure are risk factors, not guarantees of disease.

Diagnosis needs a comprehensive eye examination; pressure alone is insufficient. Examination includes optic nerve assessment, visual field testing and drainage angle inspection; corneal thickness may be measured.
Prescription drops lower pressure by reducing aqueous production or improving outflow; treatment choice depends on the person and disease type.
Laser trabeculoplasty improves drainage in open-angle glaucoma; laser iridotomy makes a small iris opening for angle-closure glaucoma.
Glaucoma surgery can create a new drainage route or use a drainage tube; pressure reduction aims to limit further nerve damage, not restore lost vision.
Follow prescribed treatment, report side effects, attend regular follow-up and do not stop glaucoma medicines without discussing with the ophthalmologist.
Sudden intense eye pain, red eye, blurred vision or nausea can signal angle closure; halos, headache and vomiting can occur. Seek urgent eye or emergency care immediately.

claims.claim: DVT is a blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the lower leg, thigh or pelvis; it can also occur in the arm.
Veins return blood from limbs and organs to the heart; a venous clot may restrict that return and cause pain and swelling.
Platelets and plasma proteins cooperate in clot formation; dangerous clots may form inside vessels without an obvious injury or fail to dissolve naturally.
Slow flow from limited movement and injury to veins can increase DVT risk; surgery and major injury are associated with higher VTE risk.
Increased estrogen and family history can raise VTE risk; risk factors do not establish a diagnosis.
DVT symptoms can include swelling, pain or tenderness, warmth, and redness or discoloration in the affected leg or arm; DVT can occur without symptoms.
Possible DVT symptoms require prompt medical evaluation; special medical tests are needed to diagnose DVT or PE.
A detached venous clot can travel through the heart to the lungs and block pulmonary blood flow, causing pulmonary embolism.
Difficulty breathing, chest pain that worsens with breathing or coughing, coughing blood, or fainting can be PE signs and require immediate medical help; PE can occur without DVT symptoms.
Anticoagulants prevent a clot from growing or spreading and prevent new clots; clot-dissolving medicines or clot removal are used in selected situations rather than for everyone.
Movement after confinement and leg exercises during long sitting can help reduce risk; individualized preventive medicines or compression stockings should be discussed with a clinician.
Damage to vein valves after DVT can cause post-thrombotic syndrome with persistent swelling, pain, skin discoloration, or ulcers in severe cases.

1. “A long, low wave” — elegant offshore profile close-up, bracket between two broad crests labelled “wavelength”; small vertical bracket labelled “wave height”; caption “A tsunami can be barely noticeable in deep water.”
2. “The whole water column” — explanatory cutaway inset with subtle distributed motion arrows from surface toward seabed. claims.claim: Tsunamis propagate through the entire water depth, unlike wind waves whose motion is concentrated near the surface.
In deep ocean water, a tsunami has a long wavelength and often small surface height; it may be barely noticeable.
Tsunami propagation speed depends on water depth: deeper water permits faster propagation; shallower water slows it.
For a long wave, propagation speed c is approximated by sqrt(g h), where g is gravitational acceleration and h water depth.
As a tsunami enters shallower water, its wavelength decreases.
Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength; slowing propagation does not itself change frequency, so wavelength becomes shorter.
Shoaling is the increase in wave amplitude as a wave moves into shallow water; tsunami waves can grow much taller near the coast.
Currents intensify as tsunamis approach shallow coastal water.
Even after shoaling, tsunami wavelengths remain relatively long; water can continue flowing inland for many minutes.
Run-up refers to the maximum height reached inland above normal sea level, distinct from horizontal inundation extent.

Chrysis ignita body length is 5–10 mm; all illustrated macro views are enlarged.
The head and mesosoma are shiny blue or violet, with green reflections on the pronotum and mesoscutellum; tergites are golden red and sternites green or blue.
The mesoscutum has punctures the same colour as the interstices; T2 and T3 have coarse regular punctation and sharply produced apical teeth.
The frontal carina of Chrysis ignita is shallowly M-shaped or arcuate, not four tooth-like tubercles.
The species occurs from western Europe to central Asia and China; distribution records can be confused by unrevised identifications.
Habitats include gardens, parks and forest margins; adults occur on old wooden or stone walls, dead tree trunks, poles and log piles.

Cuckoo wasps have a ventrally hollowed abdomen; most Chrysidinae can curl into a defensive ball (conglobulation). Females disturbed or attacked fold into a compact ball, shielding vulnerable body parts.
Chrysidid exoskeletons are heavily sculptured and very tough, providing armor against host stings; this is protection rather than invulnerability.

At family level, cuckoo-wasp immature stages include egg, larva, cocoon/pupa and adult; many develop in solitary-wasp or bee nests, as parasitoids or consumers of host provisions. Exact feeding habits differ among species.
Ancistrocerus parietum is only a probable host of Chrysis ignita; numerous earlier host records are unreliable because of inconsistent taxonomy.

claims.claim: Specific phobias involve intense fear out of proportion to actual danger; this plate applies that framework to fear of fire.
Anticipating a feared object or situation can cause excessive worry; encountering it can cause immediate intense anxiety.
People may actively avoid feared objects and situations or endure them with intense anxiety.
Phobia symptoms can include palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, dizziness and nausea.
Avoidance can restrict activities; exposure-based CBT helps people engage in activities and situations they have avoided.
CBT teaches different ways of thinking, behaving and reacting; exposure therapy is particularly effective for phobias.
Relaxation exercises may accompany exposure therapy; breathing exercises and talking to a trusted person may help manage symptoms.
Seek a primary care provider when symptoms affect life; a provider can refer to a qualified mental health professional.
Open flames are dangerous if candles tip over or are too close to combustible objects; ordinary fire precautions remain necessary.
Consider battery-operated flameless candles; lit candles need stable holders, at least 12 inches from anything that burns, and should be extinguished when leaving the room or before bed.
Use flashlights rather than candles during a power outage.

claims.claim: Aquaphobia is intense fear of water or drowning; specific phobia involves fear out of proportion to the actual danger in a particular situation.
Water exposure, thoughts of water, and reluctance to enter water or immerse the face or body can accompany fear of water; individual experiences vary.

Unfamiliar aquatic perceptive cues can accompany anxiety; a small exploratory study described concerns about depth, locating the surface, and finding solid support. These are illustrative concerns, not universal symptoms or a safety assessment.
Phobia symptoms can include severe worry, noticeable heartbeat, chest tightness, trembling, nausea, and dizziness; not everyone has every symptom.

Anticipation or encountering a feared situation can bring intense anxiety and active avoidance; phobias may interfere with daily life. The sequence illustrates repeated encounters and avoidance, not a universal causal diagnosis.
Fear of water can interfere with learning to swim and can persist into adulthood.
Natural water may have currents, waves, hidden rocks or vegetation, and limited visibility; genuine hazards should not be dismissed as anxiety.
Swimming lessons can reduce drowning risk; swimming with a buddy and choosing lifeguarded sites when possible remain important precautions.
Life jackets reduce drowning risk while boating and can help weaker swimmers around natural water and pools; inflatable or foam toys are not safety devices.

CBT is an established treatment for phobias, and exposure therapy is a particularly effective CBT method; healthcare professionals can help determine next steps. No water-entry treatment protocol is provided.
Talk to a healthcare professional if symptoms affect life. Breathing exercises and talking to someone trusted can help manage symptoms; anxiety management does not replace water safety.
The hero and dry-land help vignettes are illustrative, not a diagnosis or instruction to enter water.

claims.claim: Dental anxiety can occur before a visit; severe persistent dental fear can lead to avoidance. Ordinary nervousness does not itself establish a phobia.
Dental fear can be associated with feared pain, previous difficult experiences, unfamiliar procedures, or a perceived lack of control.
The sights of dental instruments, drilling sounds and vibrations, clinical smells, and the reclined dental-chair position can trigger anxiety for some people.
Uncertainty about what will happen can contribute to anxiety; asking questions about the procedure can help reduce fear of the unknown.
Possible anxiety responses include a noticeable heartbeat, trembling, dizziness, chest tightness, feeling sick, muscle tension and sweaty palms; symptoms vary.
Avoiding dental care can increase the risk of dental problems and make later visits more difficult, reinforcing fear; this is a possible cycle, not an inevitable outcome.
Fear can concern perceived danger; pain concerns should not be dismissed. Patients should discuss pain management and tell the dentist if pain occurs even with local anesthetic.
Tell the dental team about anxiety and previous experiences; ask what will happen and agree on a raised-hand signal to pause.
Headphones for bothersome drilling sounds, a handheld stress ball, slow breathing and relaxing tense muscles can help manage dental anxiety.
CBT and professionally guided exposure-based approaches can help with dental phobia; management should be tailored to the person and clinical situation.
Seek professional help when phobia symptoms affect life; a dentist and mental-health professional may work together on care.

claims.claim: Arachnophobia is fear of spiders, a type of specific phobia.
Phobic fear can be intense and out of proportion to actual danger.
Seeing the feared object can cause immediate anxiety; anticipation and even thinking about it can also cause anxiety.
Some people with arachnophobia avoid touching a spider; some cannot look at a spider picture.
Physical symptoms can include palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, dizziness and nausea; experiences vary.
People may actively avoid feared objects and organise life around avoidance, limiting daily activities.
A repeated encounter can provoke anxiety again; avoidance and intense anxiety are common features, not proof of actual danger.
It is not always clear why a phobia develops; frightening experiences and learned fear can be involved.
CBT is an effective treatment; exposure therapy is a CBT method particularly effective for phobias.

Breathing exercises and talking to a trusted person may help manage symptoms, and triggering images may be distressing.
Seek a primary care or qualified mental health professional when symptoms interfere with life.

claims.claim: Iron deficiency can impair production of healthy red blood cells; low hemoglobin in anemia reduces oxygen carriage from lungs to other organs.
Iron-deficiency anemia can show small red blood cells with pale centers on a blood smear; low mean cellular volume is a common laboratory finding.
Blood loss removes iron; heavy menstrual bleeding and gastrointestinal bleeding are causes requiring evaluation.
Low intake of iron-containing foods can contribute; celiac disease and stomach or intestinal surgery can impair iron absorption.
Mild or moderate iron-deficiency anemia may have no symptoms; more serious disease can cause fatigue, dizziness, pale skin, cold hands and feet, shortness of breath, or chest pain.
Evaluation includes medical and diet history, a complete blood count with hemoglobin and cell size, ferritin, and other iron studies; further testing depends on suspected cause.
Low ferritin indicates reduced iron stores; iron deficiency can occur without anemia, so hemoglobin alone does not establish iron-store status.
Treatment depends on cause and severity; clinician-guided oral iron is common, and intravenous iron may be used for poor absorption, intolerance, severe deficiency, or chronic blood loss.
Oral iron may cause upset stomach or constipation; significant symptoms should be discussed with the treating clinician.
Iron replacement must be paired with finding and treating the underlying cause; transfusion is reserved for selected severe cases and does not completely correct iron deficiency.
Beans, tofu, lean red meat, fortified cereals, and dark leafy greens provide iron; vitamin-C-rich foods such as oranges can support absorption.
Treating blood loss or absorption problems may help prevent iron-deficiency anemia; diet supports iron intake but is not a universal substitute for treatment.
Untreated iron-deficiency anemia may lead to heart problems, pregnancy complications, or developmental delays in children.

claims.claim: The pear-shaped gallbladder lies below the liver in the upper right abdomen and stores bile produced by the liver.
Bile passes through hepatic, cystic and common bile ducts into the duodenum; the pancreas also delivers digestive juices to the duodenum.
Eating signals the gallbladder to release stored bile into the duodenum to mix with food.
Gallstones are hard pebble-like material formed in the gallbladder; cholesterol stones are typically yellow-green and pigment stones are dark and made of bilirubin.

Stones may form when bile has too much cholesterol or bilirubin, insufficient bile salts, or the gallbladder empties incompletely or too infrequently; the reasons for bile changes are not fully understood.
Most gallstones are silent and do not cause symptoms; asymptomatic gallbladder stones usually need no treatment.
A stone obstructing a bile duct can cause bile buildup and biliary colic; attacks often stop when the stone moves and the blockage ends.
Pain can be severe and constant, in the upper right or middle abdomen, last several hours, and accompany nausea or vomiting; attacks often follow heavy meals.
Persistent blockage can lead to gallbladder inflammation, bile-duct infection, or gallstone pancreatitis; these are possible complications, not inevitable outcomes.
Risk is higher with older age, family history, obesity, rapid weight loss, and in women; risk factors do not establish an individual diagnosis.
Evaluation of suspected gallstones can include ultrasound and blood tests; similar symptoms may have other causes requiring clinical assessment.
The main treatment for symptomatic gallstones is gallbladder removal, often laparoscopic; ERCP may clear a stone in the common bile duct. Treatment depends on clinical circumstances.
After gallbladder removal, bile flows from the liver through the ducts directly into the duodenum rather than being stored in a gallbladder.

Healthy eating with fiber, regular physical activity, maintaining a healthy weight and avoiding rapid weight loss can help reduce gallstone risk; they do not guarantee prevention or dissolve existing stones.

Seek urgent medical care for sudden severe abdominal pain, pain lasting several hours, fever or chills, jaundice, or pain spreading to the back with vomiting; dark urine and pale stools may accompany complications.

claims.claim: A cataract is clouding of the natural lens; the normally clear lens bends incoming light to help vision.
The cornea, iris and lens are front-of-eye structures; the pupil is widened by dilation, and the retina and optic nerve are examined at the back of the eye.
The retina is the light-sensitive tissue layer at the back of the eye.
Age-related changes cause lens proteins to break down and clump, creating cloudy areas; most age-related cataracts develop gradually, at variable rates.
Cataracts can affect one or both eyes but do not spread between eyes.

Cloudy or blurry vision, faded or yellowish colors, glare or halos, difficulty seeing at night and ghosted or double images in the affected eye can occur; symptoms can also reflect other eye problems.
Older age, smoking, diabetes, sun exposure, steroid use, family history and previous eye injury are cataract risk factors; these do not establish an individual diagnosis.
Evaluation includes visual acuity or refraction, slit-lamp examination of front-of-eye structures, and a dilated examination to check the eye including retina and optic nerve.
For mild symptoms, updated glasses, brighter reading light and magnification can help function but do not remove the cataract.
Only surgery removes a cataract; the cloudy natural lens is removed and replaced by an artificial intraocular lens (IOL).
Surgery is considered when cataracts interfere with everyday activities; immediate surgery is not always needed, and benefits and risks should be discussed with an ophthalmologist.
UV-protective sunglasses and a brimmed hat, stopping smoking and protective eyewear can help reduce avoidable eye risks; these measures do not guarantee cataract prevention.
Sudden new floaters, flashes, or a curtain or shadow across vision can signal retinal detachment rather than gradual cataract change; seek an eye doctor or emergency room immediately.

claims.claim: Atopic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease, often starting in childhood but possible at any age; it is not contagious.
Barrier changes allow moisture to escape and expose the skin immune system to the environment; genes, immune activity and environmental factors contribute, and there is no single known cause.
Skin has a protective outer layer; a schematic intact-versus-disrupted surface comparison illustrates moisture retention versus increased water loss, not a literal hole through the whole skin.
Inflammation can trigger itch; scratching causes further skin damage and inflammation and increases bacterial infection risk.
Symptoms include intense itching, dryness, cracking, scaling and thickened skin; scratches may bleed or weep clear fluid.
Eczema appearance varies with skin tone: it can appear red, purple, grey or lighter or darker than surrounding skin; inflammation may leave color changes.
Common sites include elbow and knee bends and hands; babies often have facial eczema. Distribution varies by age and can occur elsewhere.
Symptoms fluctuate between flares and improvement; itch can disturb sleep.
Family history of eczema, asthma or hay fever is associated with increased likelihood, not proof of one cause.
Soap, detergents, fragrances, rough fabrics, heat and stress may worsen symptoms; triggers vary by person.
Diagnosis involves clinical skin examination and medical, family and trigger history; clinicians may use tests to rule out other causes.
Regular moisturizing, including immediately after bathing, helps retain water and supports the skin barrier; gentle unscented or non-soap cleansing and lukewarm water can help.
Avoid personal irritants, keep cool and keep nails short to reduce scratching damage; do not change diet unless advised by a clinician.

Topical corticosteroids reduce inflammation; other topical treatments, phototherapy or systemic medicines may be considered by clinicians depending on severity, age and response, not as universal treatments.
Treatment can control symptoms but there is currently no cure; seek care for symptoms or treatments that are not helping.

Painful warm swollen skin, pus, sudden worsening or spreading, fever or feeling unwell, and new blisters or leaking/crusting can signal infection or eczema herpeticum and warrant urgent medical advice.
Emollients transferred onto clothing, bedding or dressings can make fabrics catch fire more easily; avoid smoking and naked flames.
